intro: CPS-2+ is an extended version of Capcom's CPS-2 arcade system. It gives a game more program memory, more graphics, more sound samples and a larger sound program.

We made CPS-2+ for the Arrange editions of Vampire Savior, Vampire Savior 2 and Vampire Hunter 2. These editions come from Capcom's 2005 PlayStation 2 collection. Their added fighters, art and voices do not fit in the original CPS-2 memory.
Stock CPS-2 games run on CPS-2+ without change. A game uses the extensions only when it asks for them.

rows: 4 MB, encrypted, plus a 4 MB extension that is not encrypted

sections.heading: Main program
paragraphs: The original 4 MB program area stays encrypted with the game's own key. The key decrypts only part of this area, often the first 1 MB.
The extension adds 4 MB at CPU addresses A00000 to DFFFFF. This area is not encrypted. The CPU can read data and run instructions there.
The extension is not encrypted on purpose. CPS-2+ does not add a new security key, and no game gets a new key.

sections.heading: Graphics
paragraphs: The graphics memory is 64 MB. The lower 32 MB is the original graphics. The upper 32 MB is new.

A sprite selects the upper half through its object entry. The game writes the entry through a second address, an alias of the object memory. A write through the usual address selects the lower half again.
A scroll-layer tile selects the upper half with bit 9 of its attribute word. Tiles from the two halves can mix in one layer.
Rendering does not change. Flips, priorities and palettes work as they do on CPS-2.

sections.heading: Sound
paragraphs: The QSound sample memory uses a 25-bit address. A game can have 8, 16 or 32 MB of samples. The two Arrange editions use 16 MB.
The Z80 sound program can be 512 KB. The program keeps its fixed 32 KB area. One more bit in the bank register selects 30 banks of 16 KB.
The sound DSP and its program do not change.

sections.heading: How a game asks for the extensions
paragraphs: On MiSTer, the game's MRA file sends a header to the core. The header tells the core the size of each memory area. A stock game sends the stock header, and the core works as a stock CPS-2.
In HBMAME, the set definition gives the same sizes. Stock sets do not change.
A reset clears the sprite selections and the sound bank. The loaded game stays in memory.

after: Our Arrange kits include the CPS+ core, and so do the Ultra Street Fighter II and Final Fight EX (CPS-2) kits. You do not have to get it separately.
sections.heading: Where it runs
list: MiSTer: the CPS+ core, jtcps2-cpsplus_20261006.rbf. It needs a 128 MB SDRAM module. The core also plays the CPS+ arranged soundtracks.
HBMAME: the CPS+ driver, cps2plus. It runs the sets vsavs01, vsavs02, vsav2s05, vsav2s06, vhunt2s02 and vhunt2s03.
CPS-2+ games do not run on the standard jtCPS2 core or in stock MAME.

after: Each game image is about 92 MB, so it takes longer to load than a stock game.

sections.heading: For game authors
list: Put new encrypted code only in the range that the game's key decrypts. Put data anywhere.
Put new code that is not encrypted in the 4 MB extension.
Write every object entry through the alias when the sprite must use the upper graphics. Do this also for byte writes and reused slots.
Clear bit 9 of a scroll tile's attribute word for lower-half tiles. Make sure that the game does not use bit 9 for a different purpose.
Sample offsets are still 16 bits and wrap in a 64 KB bank.

sections.heading: Source and licenses
paragraphs: The CPS+ core is a GPL-3.0 fork of Jotego's jtcores. The source for this build is at github.com/strygo/jtcores, revision 9886018d.
The HBMAME driver is one class, cps2plus_state. It adds to the standard CPS-2 driver and keeps the stock behavior.

description: The 1993 Sega CD port replaced the arcade's brief story block with a fully animated opening and a soundtrack with spoken dialogue. description: Super Turbo came in two versions. Japan got Super Street Fighter II X, the one competitive players swear by. The rest of the world got a slightly different game: it plays differently, the continue screen is bare, most of the win quotes are gone, the endings are shorter, and Akuma's story is missing. description: Street Fighter Alpha 2 EX builds on our Street Fighter Alpha 2 Gold backport. Every Gold fighter plays exactly as in Gold. EX adds the menus, modes and forms the arcade game kept behind codes or never had, and every secret starts unlocked.

In CONSOLE game mode the game plays free, and START at the title opens a mode menu: Arcade, Versus, Survival, Dramatic Battle, Akuma, Training and Options. Versus matches go straight back to the select screen, and Coin opens Pause/Back on selection screens and during fights, with a confirmed Quit to the title menu. Training offers recording and replay, computer behavior and guard settings, input history and attack data. Cammy and a Random cell sit on the select screen, Cammy turns up as a CPU opponent in the other fighters' Arcade runs, and alternate forms take a START press or two instead of five.
Two EX forms join the roster, each one START press away on its fighter's cell: EX Akuma and EX Cammy. Both follow Capcom's own EX rules, with classic moves and no Super Combos.

OPTIONS opens an OPTION MODE page with difficulty, time limit, rounds, damage, turbo and sound. The operator menu adds GAME MODE, REGULATION for red or white blood, eight GAME SPEED levels and a TIME LIMIT of 25, 50, 75, 99 or infinity, and the title has a new EX mark. The USA build is in English; the Japan build, Street Fighter Zero 2 EX, keeps the Japanese. EX CONFIGURATION selects JAPAN or INTERNATIONAL backgrounds and ORIGINAL or 30TH ANNIVERSARY artwork.

The MiSTer MRAs start in CONSOLE mode. MAME and HBMAME start in ARCADE mode, which keeps Gold's arcade title; set GAME MODE to CONSOLE on the operator menu's SYSTEM page for the mode menu. It runs in MAME and HBMAME and on MiSTer.
This is a release candidate.

notes: MAME: RC4 replaces the previous default 4 MB, Modern-only audio build with an 8 MB audio build containing both Modern and Classic sound effects. It still runs in unmodified MAME as hsf2 (USA) or hsf2j (Japan); no custom MAME build is needed. Choose MODERN or CLASSIC in ULTRA CONFIGURATION. Use the newly generated ZIPs and keep them separate from original Hyper Street Fighter II ROMs. Checksum warnings are expected. HBMAME still needs the included set definitions compiled in.

Installation: install Python 3.10 or newer, extract the kit and run apply.py with your arcade ROMs, Switch game files and prod.keys. The region follows the game files you supply. Scratch and output folders are selected automatically unless you specify them. The installer checks paths before downloading tools, reports setup errors without a traceback, and groups the finished files and instructions by target. No compiler, Git, CMake, NumPy or separate FFmpeg installation is needed. For offline setup, keep cpsplus-tools-v2-offline.zip zipped and add --tools-bundle cpsplus-tools-v2-offline.zip --offline. Optional 7z inputs still need 7-Zip.

description: Street Fighter Alpha 2 wasn't the same game everywhere. In Japan, each fighter's win quote depends on who they beat and how much health they had left, and you can pick one by holding buttons. The English versions draw a few quotes at random. They also trimmed some story and ending pages, show only the country on the next-stage map, turned the blood white and left the Manual guard panel blank.

The English Restoration is the Japanese game, in English. Every win quote is back, chosen the Japanese way, and so is the button pick. The story and endings follow Japan's pages and timing, the map names the place you're headed, and the blood is red. Birdie's third victory pose and Dan's spoken line in his ending return too.

The USA version's secret fighters stay: Evil Ryu, EX Dhalsim and EX Zangief are selectable by code. The computer opponents, two-player damage and factory settings follow the Japanese version, and Charlie's Sonic Boom and Chun-Li's Kikoken get the fix from Capcom's later revision. An operator setting switches the blood to white.

There are three builds. The USA build is Street Fighter Alpha 2 in English. The Asia build is Street Fighter Zero 2 in English, with Asia's own stage details. The Japan build keeps its Japanese text and gets the same fixes and settings. All three run in MAME and HBMAME and on MiSTer.
This is a release candidate.

description: This kit brings Final Fight EX to Capcom's CPS-2 with every enhancement from the CPS-1 version. It includes a restored English version with added scenes, an improved translation and uncensored content. The test menu switches between the arcade and Sega CD cutscenes, and on MiSTer between the arranged and arcade soundtracks.

The 1993 Sega CD port of Final Fight opened with a fully animated cutscene and closed with new ending scenes, over a soundtrack with spoken dialogue. Final Fight EX brings them to the arcade game. On the CPS-2 the arcade's music and sound effects play through QSound.

The opening shows the Metro City map, the Mad Gear line-up, Damnd's sketch and the knife, Haggar's phone call and Cody and Guy. The ending adds Haggar and Jessica's reunion and Cody's farewell, and the builds made from the Japanese disc add Cody and Guy's talk in the mansion hall. CUT SCENES in the test menu switches back to the arcade's own story and ending.

On MiSTer the Sega CD's arranged soundtrack plays and the cutscenes are voiced: the USA build with the US disc's voices, the Japan build with the Japanese disc's, and the English restoration with a new English voice track. MUSIC switches back to the arcade music. In HBMAME the game plays the arcade music, and the cutscenes keep their captions.

The English restoration is the Japanese version in English: the Japanese disc's cutscenes, translated from the Japanese, with captions that follow the English voices and mouths that move with the lines.

The test menu's EX page can also turn the bonus stages off and switch the artwork to Capcom Arcade Stadium's revised soda can and Uptown sign. REGULATION chooses Jessica's outfit on Haggar's TV in the opening. A hidden stage select on the title screen can jump to any round or straight to the ending.
This is a release candidate.

projects.coverage_intro: Every soundtrack is built from one disc, one set of disks, or one album you own. Where a disc came out in several regions, the ones listed below all produce the same pack.
description: From Final Fight CD onward, Capcom kept sending its arcade soundtracks back to the studio. Every CD-based home port got a full re-recording of the music, the 'arrange' versions, produced by the original composers' teams. For thirty years those recordings stayed locked to the home versions. CPS+ puts them where they always belonged, under the arcade games themselves.

On a MiSTer, the real CPS-1 or CPS-2 hardware logic runs the game while the CD-era soundtrack plays the music, started, looped and faded by the game itself, exactly the way Capcom's own console releases timed it. Hit sounds, voices and the announcer stay pure arcade. It sounds like the arcade machine grew a CD drive.

Super Street Fighter II, Super Street Fighter II Turbo and Hyper Street Fighter II each have ten soundtracks, from the Anniversary Edition arrange to the remixed score of Ultra Street Fighter II and, new in version 1.6, the music the X68000's own FM chip played.
download_notes: The download is tools: the MRAs, the three CPS+ cores with their GPL-3.0 source, and the pack builder. It makes the packs on your machine from discs, disks and albums you own, naming anything it skips for want of a disc. It also assembles out/mister/ for you, holding the cores, your packs, and only the MRAs those packs can load, so nothing on the card fails to start.

Five MRA groups pair CPS+ audio with sets that are not stock: the Alpha 2 Gold MRAs load the SFA2 Gold reconstructed sets, the Grand Master Challenge and Super Street Fighter II EX MRAs load those projects' HBMAME sets, ‘Final Fight EX (Arrange)’ loads the Final Fight EX set, and ‘Final Fight 30th Anniversary CPS2 Edition (Arrange)’ loads the CPS2 conversion of Final Fight that the Arcade Offset project distributes. Build the first four with their own kits first (links below).
The Captain Commando MRAs change one instruction in the game, so the Stage 3 boss fight keeps its music when Yamato splits apart. Nothing else in the game differs.

a: Python 3.11 or newer, numpy, and ffmpeg on your PATH. On a Mac: brew install python ffmpeg, then pip3 install numpy. On Linux, use your package manager. 7-Zip is only needed if your rips are .7z archives. The X68000 packs, the rendered MS-DOS packs (FM, Sound Canvas and MT-32) and the USF2 Remix pack additionally need git, cmake and a C/C++ compiler (see the X68000 and USF2 questions below, and the kit's MSDOS.md). The Strider pack and the X68000 FM pack need MAME as well (see the Strider and X68000 questions).
Nothing is installed on the MiSTer itself. The kit is plain files copied to the SD card, and a stock MiSTer runs them as-is.
faq.q: What do I need installed to build the packs?

a: A .cue sheet with its .bin files beside it, a .mds/.mdf pair, or a .zip/.7z archive containing exactly one cue sheet. For the PlayStation 2 sources, point it at the .iso, a zip containing it, or a .chd. The two CD-audio sources (the Final Fight OST and the Area 88 soundtrack) are folders of .flac or .wav files instead of a disc image. The X68000 games are a zip of their .dim or .xdf floppy images. The two album sources are the downloads themselves: Capcom's Double Impact zip, as downloaded or unpacked, and the OC ReMix folder holding the FLACs. The MS-DOS game is its installed folder, or a .zip/.7z of it; the disc image alone (.cue or .chd) builds the CD soundtrack, but the FM, Sound Canvas and MT-32 packs need the installed game. The USF2 Remix pack reads the Switch game's .nsp.
Every CD source also takes a .chd, which the builder turns back into a cue sheet and image with MAME's chdman. The PlayStation 2 discs are read from their DVD .chd the same way.
faq.q: What disc rip formats does the builder accept?

a: It almost always means the disc isn't one of the supported releases listed above, or the rip is damaged. Check which release you have, re-rip if in doubt, and run make_packs.py again. A nonstandard ffmpeg build can also encode slightly differently; the stock Homebrew or distro ffmpeg matches the published hashes.
The builder won't stage a pack that fails, so a bad rip can't reach your SD card. There's a --no-verify flag if you want one anyway.
faq.q: A pack failed hash verification. What now?

a: The X68000 ports of Ghouls'n Ghosts, Street Fighter II' Champion Edition and Super Street Fighter II shipped their music as MIDI, meant for a Roland SC-55 on the desk next to the computer. There is no recording to copy, so the kit renders one on your machine, the same way the published packs were made: your disk images, your SC-55 ROM set, and a cycle-accurate SC-55 emulator built from source at a pinned revision.

That means git, cmake and a C/C++ compiler (Xcode's command-line tools on a Mac, build-essential and cmake on Debian or Ubuntu), a one-time build of a few minutes, and then ten minutes to an hour of rendering per game. The result is hash-checked like every other pack. The kit's X68000.md walks through it.

The published packs were rendered and rebuilt byte-for-byte on a Mac. Whether the emulator's output is bit-identical on every CPU has not been proven; if it isn't on yours, the builder stops at the hash check rather than staging different audio.

The Super Street Fighter II FM soundtrack is the other half of that port's music: what the X68000's own FM chip played. The kit records it by booting your disk images in MAME, opening the game's music test and playing each of its songs. It needs the same disk images, MAME, and MAME's x68000 BIOS set (x68000.zip), but no SC-55 ROMs. A few GB of disk and under an hour; the result is hash-checked like the rest. The kit's X68000.md has the details.
faq.q: What do the X68000 soundtracks need, and why are they different?

a: The PlayStation port's Sound Remix music is sequenced and played by the game's own sound driver through the console's sound chip, so there is no recording on the disc to copy. The kit makes one: MAME boots your disc, walks into the game's sound test, plays the ten performances and records the console's output. The builder then cuts the reviewed performances from that recording and checks each against its published hash.

That means MAME installed (brew install mame on a Mac, your package manager on Linux, the official build on Windows), your Strider (USA) disc as .chd or .cue, and MAME's PlayStation ROM sets, psu.zip and psx_cd.zip, in a folder you point discs.toml at. The recording takes about five minutes. The kit's PSX.md walks through it.

The pack was verified with MAME 0.288 from Homebrew on a Mac and with the official Windows build. Those two record a few samples a tiny, inaudible step apart, so the kit accepts both and checks each against its own hashes. If your MAME build renders differently, the builder stops at the hash check rather than staging different audio.
faq.q: What does the Strider pack need, and why is it different?

a: Your copy of Ultra Street Fighter II: The Final Challengers for Nintendo Switch: the USA base game's .nsp, not an update, extracted from any archive. The builder checks it against the verified file and refuses any other. It also needs your own prod.keys, which it reads where they are and never copies, and git, cmake and a C/C++ compiler: the first run builds NSTool, which reads Switch packages, and an Opus decoder.

The decoder works in fixed point, so every computer, Mac, Windows or Linux, produces the same pack and the builder can check it against one published hash. Plan on about 4 GB of free space while it runs. The kit's SWITCH.md has the details.
faq.q: What does the USF2 Remix pack need?

a: No. The CPS+ cores have their own names and the MRAs live in their own folder, so your existing cores, MRAs and ROMs are untouched. To remove it, delete the _Arcade Patches folder, the three cores and games/CPS+.
faq.q: Will this touch my existing MiSTer setup?

a: No, the kit is tools only. Every pack is made on your machine from a disc you own.
faq.q: Is any of the music in the download?

a: No. CPS+ is a MiSTer feature: the streaming player lives in the FPGA cores and the pack loads into the MiSTer's DDR memory. Everywhere else the games just play their stock music.
The companion projects do cover other targets: SFA2 Gold, Final Fight EX, Grand Master Challenge and Super Street Fighter II EX all ship HBMAME sets. See their pages, linked below.
faq.q: Do the packs work in MAME or on original arcade hardware?

a: Some of them. a: No. Every pack you built with 1.2 still works with 1.3. Three packs (the two Double Impact remixes and HD Remix) have new reference hashes, because they now build to the same bytes on every computer, but the difference is inaudible and the files are the same size. Copy the new MRAs to your card.

how_it_works: Nothing in the game is modified. CPS-1 and CPS-2 games post sound commands to their audio hardware, and the CPS+ core watches for them. When one matches the loaded pack, it streams that arranged track and holds the command back from the sound chip. Everything else plays as it always did: hit sounds, voices, the announcer, and the jingles a pack deliberately leaves alone.
The trigger tables were reverse-engineered from Capcom's own console releases and checked against the arcade programs, down to the loop points and fades.

A pack carries the arranged tracks and the table that says which sound command starts each one. The MRA points at the pack, and MiSTer loads it into memory alongside the ROM. A stock MiSTer runs all of this as it comes.
A given disc always produces the same pack, and the builder checks yours against a published hash.

projects.coverage_intro: Each game needs its cartridge ROM set and its Neo Geo CD disc, plus the Neo Geo BIOS set.
description: When Neo Geo games came to the Neo Geo CD, many of them got new soundtracks recorded for CD audio. The CD versions paid for it: long loads, and in some games animation trimmed to fit the console's memory. The cartridge games never had the arranged music.

NG+ puts the two together on a MiSTer. The cartridge game runs as it did in the arcade, with nothing cut and no loading, while the Neo Geo CD's soundtrack plays in place of the cartridge's music, started, looped and faded by the game itself. Sound effects and voices still come from the game's own sound hardware.

Version 1.1 covers 25 games: Samurai Shodown, Samurai Shodown II and III; Fatal Fury, Fatal Fury 2, Fatal Fury Special, Fatal Fury 3 and Real Bout Fatal Fury; The King of Fighters '94 and '95; Art of Fighting 2 and 3; Savage Reign, Kabuki Klash and Breakers; Top Hunter and Last Resort; Super Sidekicks, Super Sidekicks 2 and 3, Pleasure Goal, Baseball Stars 2, Top Player's Golf and Stakes Winner; and Quiz King of Fighters.
download_notes: The download is tools: the image builder with each game's published data and checksums, and the NG+ core with its GPL-3.0 source link. It builds the images on your machine from ROMs and discs you own, and assembles out/mister/, laid out like your SD card, with the core, the images and their launchers.

a: Python 3.11 or newer and ffmpeg on your PATH. A .chd disc also needs chdman, which comes with MAME. On Windows, python.org's installer and a release ffmpeg build work; run py builder\make_ngplus.py.
Nothing is installed on the MiSTer itself. The kit is plain files copied to the SD card.
faq.q: What do I need installed to build the images?

a: For the cartridge: a MAME-named zip, a Darksoft folder or zip, or a .neo file. For the disc: its .cue sheet with the images beside it, a .zip holding them, or a .chd. The BIOS is neogeo.zip, or a folder with its files.
faq.q: What ROM and disc formats does the builder accept?

a: No. The game runs from its cartridge ROMs as it did in the arcade. Only the music source changes.
faq.q: Does it change how the game plays?

a: Each game keeps its own button map and settings, under its set name, and its saves go to saves/NG+ on the card.
faq.q: Where do my settings and saves go?

a: No. The kit holds tools, checksums and the core. The builder reads the music from your own disc.
faq.q: Is any of the music in the download?

a: Almost every one. NG+ plays a CD track when the cartridge game asks for that piece of music, so a track that no cartridge music command reaches never plays. Four games have several: The King of Fighters '95 (16 tracks), Breakers (9 short pieces), Samurai Shodown III (6) and Stakes Winner (5). If you know where the Neo Geo CD version plays one of them, please get in touch.

how_it_works: Nothing in the game is modified. The Neo Geo's main processor sends sound commands to its sound processor, and the NG+ core watches for them. When one starts a song, the core streams the matching Neo Geo CD track and holds the command back, so the cartridge's own music stays quiet. Everything else plays as it always did.
The command tables come from the Neo Geo CD versions' own sound drivers and were checked against the cartridge programs, down to the loop points and fades.

The kit builds one image per game from your cartridge ROMs, your Neo Geo CD rip and your Neo Geo BIOS set, and a launcher that starts it in the NG+ core. Each image is checked against a published hash.

intro: A lot of great arcade games never made it out of Japan, and plenty of others had their best material added later, on the home ports. Re-recorded soundtracks, cutscenes the arcade version never had, characters that turned up years afterward. The patches here put that work back onto the arcade hardware it belongs on.
Each one runs against your own copy of the game, on original hardware, on a MiSTer, or in MAME. No game data is hosted here.
